conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health specialist. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s simply a way to check in on how you’re feeling emotionally now that your baby has arrived.  

Everything we discuss stays confidential, and this is a judgment-free space. The EPDS has ten questions that ask about your mood, thoughts, and experiences over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. When we’re finished, we’ll review the results together and talk about any next steps that might help you feel more supported.

Ready to begin? Thinking back over the past week, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly? Most of the time when my husband or my mom tries to joke with me, I just can’t muster a real laugh. I might force a little smile so they don’t worry, but inside it feels flat. In the past week I think I’ve actually laughed out loud maybe once—when the baby made a funny face during tummy-time—but even that felt kind of muted. Mostly I’m too tired and pre-occupied to find things funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not very often. Maybe once or twice I cracked a smile, but even when I do, it feels kind of forced—like I’m just pretending so people don’t ask what’s wrong.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk around the lake, even just binge-watching a show. This week nothing sounds worth the effort. When my sister asked me to meet her for lunch, I said yes to be polite, but I’m already dreading having to get the baby ready and leave the house.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah... pretty much every day. Yesterday the baby was fussy for hours and I kept thinking it was because I ate that spicy take-out—like I "should have known better." When he wouldn’t nap I kept replaying everything I did wrong, telling myself a "good mom" would have him on a perfect schedule. Even little stuff, like spilling a little pumped milk, makes me feel like I failed him somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah, that happens a lot. I’ll be sitting there feeding him and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s not gaining enough weight or that he’s too hot, too cold, something. I check his breathing a million times a night. There’s no real reason—his pediatrician says he’s doing great—but I can’t shake the worry.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times this week. It’s like a sudden wave—my chest gets tight, I feel shaky, and I’m convinced something awful is about to happen to the baby even though everything looks fine. I’ll rock him and tell myself it’s irrational, but in that moment I’m genuinely scared.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days. Between the night feedings, the endless laundry, and just trying to remember if I ate, it feels like I’m barely treading water. I’ll start one chore, hear him cry, drop everything to soothe him, and by the time I sit back down the whole apartment looks like a tornado hit it. I keep thinking, “I can’t do this,” but somehow I still do—yet it feels like I’m always two steps behind.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah, that’s been happening. I’ll finally get him down, crawl into bed myself, and then my brain just keeps spinning—mostly about all the ways I might be messing him up or the long list of stuff I didn’t finish. Some nights I drift off okay but wake up at 3 a.m. and can’t fall back asleep for an hour or two. It’s like the sadness just sits on my chest and won’t let me rest.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah... pretty much every day this week. I’ll be doing something routine—folding his onesies or warming a bottle—and this heaviness just settles in. I feel like I’m stuck under a gray cloud that follows me around the apartment. Some moments are worse than others, but that sad, empty feeling is almost always there in the background.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes… it’s been maybe three or four times this week. Usually it’s when I’m alone—like last night after everyone finally left and the apartment was quiet. I sat on the couch looking at the clutter and just started sobbing. I couldn’t even point to one big thing; it’s just this ache that builds up until the tears come out.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had thoughts like that. I feel overwhelmed and sad, but I haven’t wanted to hurt myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom my baby deserves.

You've shared how the joy of new motherhood feels overshadowed by a constant heaviness: laughter rarely comes, activities you once loved now feel impossible, and a cloud of sadness follows you through each day. You described feeling overwhelmed by ordinary tasks, waking in the night with racing worries, and blaming yourself for every perceived imperfection. At the same time, you experience sudden waves of fear that leave you shaky, even though your baby is healthy. Through it all you remain devoted to your child and hopeful that, with help, you can feel like yourself again.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports rare, forced laughter, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>"Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame occurring daily for multiple perceived failures, matching 'most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intense, and persistent anxiety without medical justification, aligning with "very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient experiences discrete panic episodes "a few times this week," matching "Yes, sometimes."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to keep up, and recurrent thoughts of "I can't do this," matching the guideline option indicating inability to cope most of the time.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly sleep disruption caused by persistent sadness and intrusive worries, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive daily sadness that "settles in" and feels like a constant "gray cloud," matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly reports multiple crying episodes this week, describing a persistent underlying sadness that triggers tears without a specific cause.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score places the patient well above the ≥14 threshold indicating probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>. Core symptoms map to <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: daily depressed mood (<quote>pretty much every day</quote>), markedly diminished interest (<quote>nothing sounds worth the effort</quote>), insomnia (<quote>can't fall back asleep</quote>), fatigue, feelings of worthlessness/guilt (<quote>feel like I failed him</quote>), and recurrent crying. Prominent anxiety and panic further support a mixed depression-anxiety presentation common postpartum. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med> for diagnostic confirmation and treatment planning
2. Begin evidence-based psychotherapy such as <med>interpersonal therapy</med> or <med>CBT</med> specialized for postpartum depression
3. Discuss with clinician whether an <med>SSRI</med> compatible with breastfeeding is appropriate
4. Mobilize support: ask partner or family to handle one night-feed so you can get a 4-5 hour stretch of sleep
5. Schedule brief daily walks outside with baby for natural light and gentle movement
6. Use 5-minute breathing or grounding exercises when panic sensations arise
7. Keep a simple log of mood, sleep, and anxiety spikes to review with provider
8. Provide 24/7 hotline numbers: Postpartum Support International 1-800-944-4773 and national maternal mental-health crisis line 1-833-943-5746
9. Plan follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to track response to interventions
10. Reassure yourself: reaching out shows strength and is the first step toward feeling like yourself again
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: **Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note**

**Patient-reported symptoms (past 7 days):**
- Persistent low mood, sadness, “gray cloud” most days  
- Marked anhedonia; little pleasure in previously enjoyable activities  
- Daily tearfulness (3–4 episodes)  
- Sleep-onset and mid-night awakening linked to ruminating worries  
- Pervasive guilt / self-blame regarding infant care (“good mom” perfectionism)  
- Chronic anxiety with episodic panic sensations (tight chest, shakiness, fear of harm to infant)  
- Feeling overwhelmed, “treading water,” unable to complete tasks  
- Denies self-harm ideation

**Patterns:**  
Consistent with moderate-to-severe postpartum depression with prominent anxiety features; no safety concerns voiced.

**Risk factors identified:**  
- Persistent depressive mood, anhedonia, insomnia, excessive guilt  
- Heightened postpartum anxiety/panic without precipitant  
- Functional impairment in self-care and parenting tasks  
- Absence of suicidal ideation (noted for ongoing monitoring)

**Screening impression:**  
Elevated score consistent with probable major postpartum depression and comorbid anxiety; warrants immediate comprehensive clinical evaluation and follow-up for diagnostic clarification and treatment planning.
